stories.title: Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men
stories.titleZh: 中年男性自杀率创历史新高

comments.author: munificent
comments.textRawHtml:
Because it's highly relevant, I'm going to paraphrase a comment I made last week:

I think a big part of the problem is that middle-aged men are at the apex of their expectations to be successful in the eyes of society, and we are living through a period of time where success is very hard to define, much less attain.

There is a name for this in sociology: anomie [1]. Émile Durkheim coined it in his book Suicide, written not too long after the Industrial Revolution.

In times of great change, the set of norms and rules that we take for granted as an organizing principle of our lives get uprooted. It's as if all of the pieces and tokens and rules of the board game we played our whole lives are swept off the table to make room for a new game, but the new game has not been set up yet. In that interim, we all feel a sense of unease. It is our turn to move, but we don't know the rules of the game or what moves to make. We feel intense pressure to play the game well, but don't know how.

In the past, these transitions have ended and society has generally returned to some sense of stability. A new board game gets set up, new pieces doled out, we learn to play the new game. I hope we get to that point with AI soon, but the revolutions seem to keep coming faster and faster.

I think for a lot of men, it feels like just at the time when we should be able to rest on our laurels a bit after having worked so hard to play the game society told us to, the rules have been ripped out from under us and any sense of security going forward is lost. We feel too old to learn the new rules of the game in time to play well, but not old enough to be able to abstain from playing.

It's a psychologically very difficult time.

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomie
comments.textZhHtml:
因为它非常相关，所以我将解释一下我上周发表的评论：

我认为问题的很大一部分在于，在社会眼中，中年男性正处于他们对成功的期望的顶峰，而我们正在经历一个很难定义成功的时期，更不用说实现了。

社会学中有一个名字：失范[1]。埃米尔·涂尔干 (Émile Durkheim) 在工业革命后不久写的《自杀》一书中创造了这个词。

在巨大变革的时代，我们视为理所当然的生活组织原则的一套规范和规则被连根拔起。就好像我们一生玩过的棋盘游戏的所有棋子、令牌和规则都被扫出了桌子，为新游戏腾出空间，但新游戏还没有建立起来。在此期间，我们都感到不安。轮到我们走棋了，但我们不知道游戏规则，也不知道该走什么棋。我们感受到要玩好游戏的巨大压力，但不知道如何去做。

过去，这些转变已经结束，社会总体上恢复了某种稳定感。一个新的棋盘游戏被设置，新的棋子被分发，我们学习玩新游戏。我希望人工智能很快就能达到这一点，但革命似乎会越来越快。

我认为，对于很多人来说，感觉就像是在我们辛辛苦苦玩了社会告诉我们的游戏之后，应该能够在功劳簿上休息一下的时候，规则已经被从我们身上撕下来，任何前进的安全感都消失了。我们觉得自己太老了，无法及时学习新的游戏规则来玩好游戏，但还没有老到能够戒掉游戏。

这是一个心理上非常困难的时期。

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomie

children.author: monknomo
children.textRawHtml:
Well said! 5 years ago I could have a pretty solid picture of what my career would look like through retirement.

Today, unclear what that would look like as well as unclear if the career will even exist that long.

One sunny spot I have is that life is very long. I think I have 1.5 careers left in me, and a full pivot is alright. I've been talking with older folks, and loads of people have historically done giant pivots at midlife.
children.textZhHtml:
说得好！ 5 年前，我可以非常清楚地了解退休后我的职业生涯会是什么样子。

今天，我不清楚那会是什么样子，也不清楚职业生涯是否会存在那么久。

我有一个阳光明媚的地方，那就是生命很长。 我想我还剩下1.5个职业生涯，完全转向就可以了。 我一直在与老年人交谈，历史上有很多人在中年时做过巨大的转变。

children.author: georgemcbay
children.textRawHtml:
> One sunny spot I have is that life is very long.

Not sure exactly where you are in it, but as a 53 year old I disagree. The younger I was the less likely I would have been to disagree but imo/ime the older you get the faster it feels like it is flying by.

> and a full pivot is alright

The AI-related existential dread is that it is very unclear what a pivot looks like when the ground under everything is shifting all at once.

The shifting is certainly a lot more obvious in our career than some others, but all of that shift (so far) happened more or less in a mere 10 months and is accelerating. And I don't think it is very likely that our career will stay anomalous for very long in terms of how much AI impact there is.
children.textZhHtml:
> 我有一个阳光的地方，那就是生命很长。

不确定你到底处于哪个位置，但作为一个 53 岁的人，我不同意。我越年轻，我就越不可能不同意，但在我看来，你年纪越大，感觉就像飞过的速度越快。

>并且一个完整的枢轴是好的

与人工智能相关的存在恐惧是，当一切的基础都在同时发生变化时，我们不清楚枢轴是什么样子。

这种转变在我们的职业生涯中肯定比其他一些人更明显，但所有这些转变（到目前为止）或多或少都发生在仅仅 10 个月，而且还在加速。 而且我认为，就人工智能的影响力而言，我们的职业生涯不太可能长期保持异常状态。

children.author: monknomo
children.textRawHtml:
yeah, you're down to like 3/4 a career left, it makes sense that you feel that way. Less runway ought to feel different.

I do agree that a safe 'next' is unclear. But I also think if ai truly hits all knowledge work as hard as it might we're looking at up to 50% unemployment. Frankly there is no point career planning at all in that scenario. We will all have much larger problems.

And if it doesn't, then pivoting to some field with a combination of rewarding work and 'enough' pay seems sensible enough.

children.author: bigstrat2003
children.textRawHtml:
> One sunny spot I have is that life is very long. I think I have 1.5 careers left in me, and a full pivot is alright.

I'm 41 and I could, in theory, pivot. But realistically: I'm good at exactly one thing in this world in terms of job ability. I can cook, I can bake, I can play music, but none nearly well enough to actually make a living on it. Thus the end of my tech career, if it should come to pass, basically means I will have to work menial jobs to get by. The future is very bleak for me, and the only real hope is that the tech industry will wake up to what a bad job LLMs do compared to humans. But while I think they will do that eventually, there's no telling how long it will take, and the thought that the market will eventually correct is cold comfort if I can't get a job in the meantime.

comments.author: a11r
comments.textRawHtml:
Artificial analysis shows this: underperforming Qwen3.8 Flash Next and GLM 5.3 Flash, both of which you can run on a single B300 . I think Meta has a bit of catching up to do in the open-weight space.

As an aside, it's really unfortunate that artificial analysis only provides comparison at the highest reasoning level, which is mostly unusable for high-volume production use cases. I would really like them to start providing comparisons at low and medium reasoning levels across these models because those tend to be the ones that actually get used in production.
comments.textZhHtml:
人工分析表明：Qwen3.8 Flash Next 和 GLM 5.3 Flash 的性能较差，这两者都可以在单个 B300 上运行。我认为 Meta 在开放权重领域还需要迎头赶上。

顺便说一句，人工分析只能提供最高推理级别的比较，这对于大批量生产用例来说几乎无法使用，这确实很不幸。我真的希望他们开始在这些模型中提供中低推理水平的比较，因为这些模型往往是实际在生产中使用的模型。

children.author: deepsun
children.textRawHtml:
Don't forget the compounding effect. Say, one country (or city or community) decides to invest their efforts into area X (e.g. clock making in Switzerland). They do it and become better and better. As long as they keep doing that they can become #1 in the world. Regardless of any reasons "why them".

There's no reason Netherlands are better at chip lithography except that they're doing it (Dutch agriculture success can be attributed to good soils/climate/geolocation, but not chips). There's no reason Hollywood is better at filmmaking. Kinda chaos theory -- small changes to initial state leads to huge changes in the later outcomes.
children.textZhHtml:
不要忘记复合效应。比如说，一个国家（或城市或社区）决定将其精力投入到 X 领域（例如瑞士的钟表制造）。他们这样做并且变得越来越好。只要他们继续这样做，他们就能成为世界第一。不管“为什么”有任何原因。

荷兰没有理由在芯片光刻方面做得更好，除非他们正在这样做（荷兰农业的成功可以归因于良好的土壤/气候/地理位置，但不是芯片）。好莱坞没有理由更擅长电影制作。有点混沌理论——初始状态的微小变化会导致后来结果的巨大变化。

The Hollywood case has a quirk that is relevent to the extensional content of HN:

West coast filmmakng started in the Bay Area (at the time the largest conurbation in the west) but moved south because of the year 'round weather.

But why the west? Because Edison controlled the filmmaking patents and demanded not just royalties but script oversight as well. By moving west, they could ignore the patents because they were simply too hard to enforce from such a long distance.

So ironically, given how things worked out, IP piracy is at the root of Hollywood.

西海岸电影制作始于湾区（当时是西部最大的城市），但由于全年天气而向南移动。

但是为什么是西部呢？ 因为爱迪生控制着电影制作专利，不仅要求版税，还要求剧本监督。 通过向西转移，他们可以忽略这些专利，因为从这么远的距离执行这些专利太难了。

具有讽刺意味的是，考虑到事情的发展，知识产权盗版是好莱坞的根源。

I've been using OpenCode V2 since it first appeared on the website, and I can only repeat the positive views on usability, the client/server model and self-awareness/ability to edit it's config and write plugins.

I'd like to mention two other impressive things about OpenCode.

First, their issue tracker on GitHub works really well. They have the OpenCode GitHub App connected, and for any bug report it reads the issue, tests on the mentioned version and latest dev branch, and comments the findings along with a reproduction script. For TUI Bugs it even records a video. And all that in less than two minutes, usually.

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues?q=is%3Aissue+st...

Another thing they are working on is opentunnel, where you can tunnel services to https on <random>.opentunnel.xyz and its subdomains. What's notable is that the subdomain is persistent and unique to you, and a wildcard ssl cert is actually generated on your machine, so the platform cannot see the traffic. Their primary use case seems to be making the OpenCode Server usable from anywhere, but it can do much more with their cli:

https://opentunnel.xyz/

comments.author: solarkraft
comments.textRawHtml:
It's good.

Many of the annoyances from V1 are gone. Skills and plugins reload automatically (finally). Tasks can be backgrounded (though I think this doesn't happen automatically yet). There's a built-in skill for editing the configuration (finally I can retire mine). The front-end got some love. Apparently they re-architected the loop around Effect. Sub-sessions can be communicated with better. Configuration is loaded from the folder the session is created in rather than where the server was started.

In general, this update largely takes OpenCode into the current age features-wise and is a good overhaul quality-wise. Just in time to stop my early switching away efforts, which would've been a pain because I know few other harnesses with such a strong server/client model.

Pi notably ships without MCP support (or it did, I can't remember if they're adding it to Pi main or just the durable one). From a vanilla Pi perspective, I'm pretty sure but not positive that it can't. It would have to install an MCP plugin, and you would have to re-launch Pi to load that plugin.

It does have native tools, but they're also in plugins that aren't hot-reloaded. The LLM would have to write the tool, you close Pi and re-open it before it was available.

> Would you consider that a gap in security posturing?

Honestly, I think trying to secure the harness is a lost cause for the same reasons SELinux never really took off. They solve a real problem in a way so painful people would rather just live dangerously.

I actually wrote a thing to implement my security posture https://github.com/SethCurry/abyss TLDR it pretends to be an ACP agent, but runs the agent inside Docker (with optional bind mounts) and proxies the ACP connection into the container.

I'm also tinkering with WASM-based plugins in the ACP proxy to add some additional security and compliance posturing at the protocol layer (ie agnostic to what the underlying agent is). E.g. I slapped together a plugin that will automatically cancel a prompt mid-turn if an OpenRouter API token shows up in a) the prompt, b) agent output/thinking, c) agent tool calls. ([1], [2], [3]). The grand vision is slapping centralized management on that so security and compliance teams get a "firewall" of sorts to prevent leaking secrets, filter bash commands, censor PII, yada, yada.

children.author: everforward
children.textRawHtml:
I looked and will give it a try, but haven’t had a chance yet because life.

I had debated building something like this, and I really want to see what the other fork in the path looks like.

One of the core tenants of mine is to not impose a workflow or set of tooling on the user. I specifically opted not to go with k8s because access to local files is going to be a pain, and I think people will still expect that. There’s all sorts of “I need this binary that’s not in APT”, or “you need this cert to test, and we can’t commit it” stumbling blocks.

Yours feels like it’s pushing me into an unfamiliar workflow, but opinionated tools are often better so it’s worth a try.

My only direct criticism is that I think k8s is a bad way to go for this (but is probably what people expect). For personal use, k8s is more than I want to deal with. For work use, I suspect lambdas would be cheaper and avoid a ton of maintenance junk. We tend to think of agents as a persistent process, but they’re sort of not. They’re a stateless process that is effectively dead until a new message comes in, let it be dead until something else comes down the pipe.

children.textRawHtml:
Given how expensive this computation would have been in 1997, it makes perfect sense they'd taken months, but even if we assume they tried all timestamps of 1997 and selected arbitrarily among the first 16 viable candidate of any timestamp, that's just ~30 bits of freedom.

Finding out there is a class of weak 256-bit elliptic curves so large that they can be hit randomly with 2^30 tries would be a cryptanalytic breakthrough analogous to discovering all elliptic curve cryptography is broken.

Read section 3.1 of the Koblitz and Menezes paper. It was already implausible with 160 bits of freedom. https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/1018

If you want to believe the NSA knows ECC is broken and chose to risk moving the US government to it and somehow no one figured out the same break in 30 years, you're free to do so. But pretending the seed choice plays any role in that theory is over.

children.author: cyphar

Almost all of the smaller values of n are not valid curve values, so they were searching "harder" but just for valid seeds. If you look at the generator output in [1], you'll see that:

1. Only a very small number of valid seeds were discarded when compared to the number of n values. It seems we don't yet know why about half of the valid seeds were discarded but the explanation of a buggy curve validity checker doesn't seem implausible to me.

This has been my argument for the past few weeks to explain why we aren’t seeing or feeling real world productivity gains as consumers despite many espousing the efficiency of AI they personally see with their own workflows. The hands on work is rarely the actual bottleneck.

My team can crank out high quality work in a few hours and AI could do the same medium to high quality work in a minute or two, but the review, feedback, and sign off takes days of back and forth. AI just slows this part of the process down because editing AI work is often a challenge because, no one is quite as familiar with how it was put together and sometimes it creates things that are not editable at all. And telling AI to make very specific changes is often a mixed bag at best.

Solo devs and small teams with minimal oversight can probably move a lot faster, but corporations are going to see minimal uplift except in areas where no one is looking.
children.textZhHtml:
这一直是我在过去几周的论点，以解释为什么我们作为消费者没有看到或感受到现实世界的生产力提高，尽管许多人拥护他们亲眼所见的人工智能在自己的工作流程中的效率。动手工作很少是真正的瓶颈。

我的团队可以在几个小时内完成高质量的工作，人工智能可以在一两分钟内完成相同的中等到高质量的工作，但审查、反馈和签署需要几天的时间来回。人工智能只是减慢了这部分过程，因为编辑人工智能工作通常是一项挑战，因为没有人非常熟悉它是如何组合在一起的，有时它会创建根本无法编辑的东西。告诉人工智能做出非常具体的改变往往是一个好坏参半的问题。

独立开发者和监督最少的小团队可能会移动得更快，但除了无人关注的领域之外，企业将看到最小的提升。

Established successful companies operate in a world where action and change often introduce more immediate risk than staying still. In those companies AI doesn't necessarily offer a lot of "increased productivity" gains because writing the code isn't the bottleneck. But many of them will try to chase cost savings by laying people off or slowing hiring.

There's a couple types of companies where the reverse is true: young companies trying to grow, and dying ones that need a turnaround.

Out of those two, young companies are less likely to be set in their ways. So the first place you really see the result of development moving faster with AI is probably going to be in future months and years when suddenly-big companies start getting widely known with products and business strategies that wouldn't have made sense a decade ago because writing code to try different things to even get the ball rolling was a bottleneck, and you could only do things that wouldn't scale for so long.
children.textZhHtml:
对于成熟的成功公司来说，行动和变革往往比保持静止会带来更直接的风险。在这些公司中，人工智能不一定会带来很多“提高生产力”的收益，因为编写代码并不是瓶颈。但他们中的许多人会试图通过裁员或放慢招聘速度来节省成本。

有几种类型的公司情况恰恰相反：年轻的公司试图发展，而垂死的公司需要扭亏为盈。

在这两种公司中，年轻的公司不太可能按自己的方式行事。因此，你第一个真正看到 AI 带来的更快发展的结果可能是在未来的几个月和几年里，那时大公司突然开始以十年前没有意义的产品和业务策略而广为人知，因为编写代码来尝试不同的事情甚至让事情滚动是一个瓶颈，你只能做一些无法长期扩展的事情。

The internet "existed" in the late 80's, early 90's. Many companies are still reaping productivity gains from plugging into this first.

children.author: lumost
children.textRawHtml:
I work in code generation, and often feel the fallacy of “because I can build something that looks 80% like your product in a day, you should pay me N millions.”

It's roughly the same pitch that the ruby on rails crowd had 15 years ago, and the no code crowd 5 years ago.

Very few companies need to rebuild their product every week, or actually care what tech stack it runs on. They are trying to build new things, or reduce how often those things break, or figuring out what if anything is worth building next.
children.textZhHtml:
我从事代码生成工作，经常感到这样的谬论：“因为我可以在一天内构建出与您的产品看起来 80% 相似的东西，您应该付给我 N 百万美元。”

这与 15 年前的 Ruby on Rails 人群和 5 年前的无代码人群的宣传大致相同。

很少有公司需要每周重建他们的产品，或者真正关心什么技术堆栈它继续运行。他们正在尝试构建新的事物，或者减少这些事物损坏的频率，或者弄清楚下一步是否值得构建什么。

children.author: thelastgallon
children.textRawHtml:
> Solo devs and small teams with minimal oversight can probably move a lot faster

Spot on!

Usually, most work in corps is slowed down by executive decisions. It takes 3 - 9 months to get a yes/no on something and for most things that are obvious that need to be done need to go up the chain of command. The decision takes forever, but when the decision is made, they want things to be done quickly, which creates unreasonable stress on the ICs.

The first step to see real productivity gains is for AI to eliminate the executive and middle-management layer, this starts a virtuous cycle, destroys both empire building and massively accelerates true productivity, not just meaningless metrics like LOC.
children.textZhHtml:
> 单独的开发人员和监督最少的小团队可能会进展得更快

完全正确！

通常，团队中的大多数工作都会因执行决策而减慢。需要 3 - 9 个月的时间才能对某件事做出是/否的决定，对于大多数明显需要完成的事情，都需要向上级指挥。决策需要很长时间，但当决策做出后，他们希望事情能够快速完成，这对 IC 造成了不合理的压力。

看到真正生产力提升的第一步是人工智能消除执行层和中层管理层，这会启动一个良性循环，破坏帝国建设并大幅加速真正的生产力，而不仅仅是像 LOC 这样毫无意义的指标。

children.author: somenameforme
children.textRawHtml:
Speaking realistically, you're going in the wrong direction here. The most likely scenario in the short run is that management will seek to replace labor with automated systems supported by a skeleton crew to aid in implementation and execution level tasks that can't (or shouldn't) be handled by the LLM alone, like deployment.

So the first signs of productivity gains will be shrinking head count, but it's going go from the bottom up, as usual.
children.textZhHtml:
说实话，你在这里走错了方向。短期内最有可能的情况是，管理层将寻求用由骨干人员支持的自动化系统取代劳动力，以帮助实施和执行级别的任务，这些任务不能（或不应该）由法学硕士单独处理，例如部署。

因此，生产力提高的第一个迹象将是减少员工人数，但它会像往常一样从下到上进行。

I considered it an absolute win when I submitted an LLM assisted PR that removed 30k LOC :)

> most work in corps is slowed down by executive decisions

I work in a startup and I find it to be the opposite. Management wants us to go really fast and engineering is like "well wait we should slow down because just because LLMs can write a bunch of code doesn't mean it can build a maintainable app"

That said, I know that our small engineering team can't build an entire business by ourselves. So some management is required. But as you said, getting stuff done quickly is stressful. And with LLMs we're expected to get a LOT of stuff done very quickly. Some colleagues have decided to go on quiet strike by submitting AI slop and citing "no time to review" to prove a point. I don't fault them, but I also know that me and someone else will have to clean up their messes at some point.
children.textZhHtml:

children.author: weinzierl
children.textRawHtml:
I know the Doorman Fallacy is an established concept, but where did it really ever apply? The automatic door has won despite, devastatingly so (and no your fancy upper east side building doesn't count and neither does the Regency or the Hilton).

The doorman was called a doorman because its essential task was the door. Everything else was additional and replaceable or unnecessary in the first place.

Same with AI. Once it has replaced the main task, the rest will adapt around it.
children.textZhHtml:
我知道门卫谬误是一个既定的概念，但它真正适用于哪里？尽管如此，自动门还是取得了毁灭性的胜利（不，你那精美的上东区建筑不算在内，摄政酒店或希尔顿酒店也不算在内）。

门卫被称为门卫，因为它的基本任务是门。首先，其他一切都是额外的、可替换的或不必要的。

人工智能也是如此。一旦它取代了主要任务，其余的就会围绕它进行调整。

children.author: CodeyWhizzBang
children.textRawHtml:
When you say the automatic door "has won" do you mean it's won by rendering doormen obsolete? Because if so, that seems very untrue. According to Vanity Fair and NPR there are over 25,000 doormen working in New York City. 1930 there were an estimated few thousand. So since the invention of the automatic door, the number of doormen has skyrocketed.

Maybe, you'd say there are more automatic doors than doormen. I'm confident that is true, but those automatic doors haven't supplanted doormen; they're automatic doors where there would have been manual doors before.

So everything hasn't adapted around automatic doors. We've just got a lot more automatic doors now. And a lot more doormen.

comments.textRawHtml:
This is a really enjoyable take, pushing the feeling of what one does on a computer towards actually being at a desk and having to reach for various functions. I feel like that would enable spatial memory to do some cool things.

I miss the 90s chunkiness of switches, buttons, hardware: being able to hear the computer "think" (HDD seeks), the hum of a CRT. Modern machinery feels so insubstantial, emphasizing clean glass and tidy machined chassis. (chassies?)

I have this persistent daydream about a computer setup that feels like the Nostromo flight deck from Alien. I almost want to feel like I'm sitting _inside_ a computer when I'm at my desk, surrounded by powerful feeling electronics with substantial switches and such. Of course there's plenty of inconvenience there too, but something about it appeals to me.
comments.textZhHtml:
这是一种非常令人愉快的体验，将人们在计算机上所做的事情的感觉推向了实际坐在办公桌前并必须伸手去操作各种功能的感觉。我觉得这将使空间记忆能够做一些很酷的事情。

我怀念 90 年代厚重的开关、按钮、硬件：能够听到计算机“思考”（HDD 寻找）、CRT 的嗡嗡声。现代机械感觉如此虚无，强调干净的玻璃和整洁的机加工底盘。 （底盘？）

Also, you can’t praise an amazing service that takes insane amounts of r&d money to bring to market in the same breath as complaining about giving money to massive corporations. No two guys in a garage are starting a self-driving car company or a supersonic jet company by themselves. Massive capital is required to launch satellites, build cars, build datacenters, etc.

此外，你不能一边抱怨向大公司提供资金，一边赞扬一项需要大量研发资金才能推向市场的出色服务。 车库里没有两个人能够独自创办一家自动驾驶汽车公司或一家超音速喷气式飞机公司。 发射卫星、制造汽车、建设数据中心等都需要大量资金。

children.author: rcxdude
children.textRawHtml: Enshittification is generally an exploitation of market efficiencies in some form, be it lock-in effects or market dominance in an area with a high barrier to entry. It's an explicit goal of a lot of investment: pick one company in an area, invest so much money into it no-one else can compete, corner the market by offering a better product than anyone else, then once you own the market, turn up the price and turn down the quality to get as much money out of it before someone builds a competitor and your customers can leave.
children.textZhHtml: Enshittification 通常是以某种形式利用市场效率，无论是锁定效应还是在进入壁垒较高的领域的市场主导地位。这是大量投资的明确目标：在一个领域选择一家公司，向其中投入大量资金，让其他人无法竞争，通过提供比其他任何人更好的产品来垄断市场，然后一旦你拥有了市场，就提高价格并降低质量，以便在有人建立竞争对手并且你的客户离开之前从中获取尽可能多的钱。

stories.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
stories.titleZh: Claude Code 团队如何进行代码审查

comments.author: avinoth
comments.textRawHtml:
This is like one of Google’s infrastructure blog. Google scale things are only relevant and appropriate for them. We had lots of bitter lessons from smaller engineering teams following the process with the justification that “this is how Google does it”.

Similarly, Anthropic can afford to do this because they have virtually unlimited tokens and labs to train models for their specific usecase. The rest of us need code comprehension lest we become dependent on continuous supply of tokens (which is a state these labs badly want to achieve)

So, unless you work at a lab, or have unlimited tokens guaranteed through the life of your company, it would do both the company and you good to continue to read the code and not let these 30k PRs per engineer be the norm.

An excerpt from the article makes my point

> Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.
comments.textZhHtml:
这就像 Google 的基础设施博客之一。谷歌规模的东西只与他们相关并且适合他们。我们从较小的工程团队那里吸取了很多惨痛的教训，他们遵循的过程是“谷歌就是这样做的”。

同样，Anthropic 也有能力做到这一点，因为他们拥有几乎无限的代币和实验室来训练针对其特定用例的模型。我们其他人需要代码理解，以免我们变得依赖于持续供应代币（这是这些实验室非常希望实现的状态）

因此，除非您在实验室工作，或者在公司的整个生命周期内保证拥有无限的代币，否则继续阅读代码而不是让每个工程师 30k PR 成为常态，对公司和您都有好处。

文章的摘录表明了我的观点

>团队成员的头脑中保留着 Claude Code 的完整心理模型，我们认为任何人都不需要这样做。当有人想要理解代码库的一部分时，他们会要求 Claude 为该部分编写一个解释器。它需要几分钟的时间并反映当前的代码。

children.author: thatsabadlook
children.textRawHtml:
Even then do we really have evidence that what they are doing is reasonable or practical for them at all? They are edging on like 3 9s uptime, what leaked of Claude code looked like soup, tons of security issues, they can't build a sandbox to save their company, and last I heard they aren't even profitable without adjusting their numbers for arbitrary things.

Think I'm good on taking advice from companies that aren't making money.
children.textZhHtml:
即便如此，我们真的有证据表明他们所做的事情对他们来说是合理的或实用的吗？他们的正常运行时间接近 3 个 9，泄露的克劳德代码看起来像汤，大量的安全问题，他们无法构建沙箱来拯救他们的公司，最后我听说，如果不调整任意事情的数字，他们甚至无法盈利。

我认为我很擅长听取不赚钱的公司的建议。

children.author: avinoth
children.textRawHtml: Exactly. What they’re doing, repeatedly, is setting a narrative that this is how software engineering should be. Always be reliant on tokens. Don’t worry about uptime or errors - agents can address it, don’t worry about security - agents can address it, don’t worry about code comprehension - agents will always be there for you.
children.textZhHtml: 正是如此。他们不断地重复着这样的故事：软件工程就应该是这样的。始终依赖代币。不用担心正常运行时间或错误 - 代理可以解决它，不用担心安全性 - 代理可以解决它，不用担心代码理解 - 代理将永远为您服务。

children.author: oblio
children.textRawHtml:
> agents will always be there for you.

In Romania an investment fund (FNI) around 2000 ran some super famous ads saying "FNI is watching" (FNI is keeping watch).

6 months later they went bankrupt.

> 代理商将永远为您服务。

2000 年左右，罗马尼亚的一家投资基金 (FNI) 投放了一些超级著名的广告，上面写着“FNI is Watch”（FNI 正在注视）。

6 个月后，他们破产了。

children.author: panarky
children.textRawHtml:
If they're cash-flow positive with 75% of compute going to research and training, what do you think will happen to cash flow when they shift to 50-50 training-inference?

Because "pacing the frontier" is more about flipping on the money printer switch than it is about safety.
children.textZhHtml:
如果他们的现金流为正，75% 的计算用于研究和培训，那么您认为当他们转向 50-50 训练推理时，现金流会发生什么？

因为“调整前沿”更多的是打开印钞机开关，而不是安全。

children.author: thr0w
children.textRawHtml:
> they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice

If their Claude is the same as our Claude, then this is a joke. Claude’s writing style is insidiously mind numbing. It takes constant pushing to get it to explain things in digestible English.
children.textZhHtml:
> 他们要求克劳德为那个切片写一个解释器

如果他们的克劳德和我们的克劳德一样，那么这是一个笑话。克劳德的写作风格令人心智麻木。需要不断地推动它才能用易于理解的英语解释事物。

children.author: bulbar
children.textRawHtml:
It also mixes important with unimportant information. It tends to think that a commit/bugfix is important and will happily list it together with important properties of the feature.

At least Opus 5.5 does that. Its writing is better than that if other models, though. I had other models explain stuff in an undigestable language, technically correct, but practically not what anything is about.
children.textZhHtml:
它还混合了重要和不重要的信息。它倾向于认为提交/错误修复很重要，并且很乐意将其与功能的重要属性一起列出。

至少 Opus 5.5 做到了这一点。不过，它的写作比其他模型要好。我让其他模型用难以理解的语言解释了一些东西，技术上是正确的，但实际上并不是什么内容。

children.author: engine_y
children.textRawHtml:
It's like it's trying to impress you with poetry in comment: 
"What the function does, it does well, and only just once"
children.textZhHtml:
它就像试图用评论中的诗歌来打动你： 
“该函数的作用是，它做得很好，而且只执行一次”

children.author: froggy
children.textRawHtml: Try having it explain something in “ISO Plain Language standard”. It made an enormous difference for me yesterday. The language will change from dense large paragraphs to simply-worded 2-3 sentence paragraphs. I was using gpt though.
children.textZhHtml: 尝试让它解释“ISO 普通语言标准”中的某些内容。昨天这对我来说发生了巨大的变化。语言将从密集的大段落变为措辞简单的2-3句段落。不过我使用的是 gpt。

children.author: meheleventyone
children.textRawHtml: Even getting it to write less obtuse English isn't enough IMO. It seems to have real issues with structuring documentation in a way that makes it easy to follow. Also it's a real demon for leaking its context as implicit assumptions into documentation.
children.textZhHtml: 在我看来，即使让它写得不那么迟钝的英语也是不够的。以易于理解的方式构建文档似乎存在真正的问题。此外，它也是一个真正的恶魔，会将其上下文作为隐式假设泄露到文档中。

children.author: panarky
children.textRawHtml: v5.5 eliminated much of the impenetrable prose of earlier versions.
children.textZhHtml: v5.5 消除了早期版本中许多难以理解的散文。

children.author: thr0w
children.textRawHtml:
> v5.5

You don't still feel that mental friction when 5.5 responds with a wall of text and you drop into that first tedious sentence? I even had it generate a syntactically invalid English sentence the other day. It's still pretty bad.
children.textZhHtml:
> v5.5

当 5.5 用一堵文字墙回应并且你陷入第一个乏味的句子时，你是否仍然感到精神上的摩擦？前几天我什至让它生成了一个语法无效的英语句子。还是很糟糕。

children.author: wowoc
children.textRawHtml: It’s better, but still worse than OAI’s models in my experience
children.textZhHtml: 根据我的经验，它比 OAI 的模型更好，但仍然较差

children.author: mbel
children.textRawHtml: Or we’re just getting used to it.
children.textZhHtml: 或者我们只是习惯了。

children.author: Starlevel004
children.textRawHtml: The people who work at Claude seem to talk in claudlish, so I doubt they care.
children.textZhHtml: 在克劳德工作的人似乎用克劳德语说话，所以我怀疑他们在乎。

children.author: mrits
children.textRawHtml: If we as engineers didn't use similar terminology to describe any code not written by ourselves for the last few decades perhaps people would take it seriously.
children.textZhHtml: 如果我们作为工程师不使用类似的术语来描述过去几十年里任何不是我们自己编写的代码，也许人们会认真对待它。

children.textZhHtml: 克劳德接受过工程 wittering 培训。
